steps.hypothesis: Question: for this element-set-disjoint split, (a) does the 86-dim stoichiometry vector C carry information beyond the 81 summary elemental descriptors X, (b) how much of development error is irreducible (repeated/contradictory compositions) or within-element-set (stoichiometry-resolving) rather than between-set, (c) is error concentrated in the high-Tc (cuprate-like) tail with systematic shrinkage bias, and (d) does error grow with chemical distance (Jaccard element overlap / composition distance) to the nearest training element set? Evidence: only three measured baselines exist (median RMSE 36.04, Ridge 18.11, HGB 13.38 on development); nothing is known yet about where HGB's 13.38 K comes from, so any representation or objective change would be an unguided parameter variation. Contrasting expected outcomes that would change my next move: (1) if HGB on C alone is close to HGB on X, chemistry identity — not the averaged property descriptors — carries the signal, favoring learned element embeddings over more descriptor engineering; if C alone is far worse, X's weighted property statistics are the transferable carrier and C mainly memorizes elements that cannot transfer to unseen sets; (2) if the dev oracle 'predict the element-set mean' RMSE is a large fraction of total dev RMSE, between-set transfer is the bottleneck and group-aware/ hierarchical modeling matters; if it is small, within-set stoichiometry resolution dominates and per-row composition features matter more; (3) if the exact-duplicate-composition RMSE floor is a sizeable share of 13.4 K, part of the remaining gap is measurement inconsistency, not model capacity, and RMSE improvements beyond that floor should be treated skeptically; (4) if squared error is dominated by y>=50 K rows with strong negative bias (shrinkage), a two-regime or transformed-target objective is indicated, whereas log1p being worse in RMSE would rule out that route; (5) if group MAE correlates strongly with 1 - max Jaccard overlap to training element sets, an explicit distance-aware/extrapolation-robust method (or distance-weighted validation) is justified, whereas a near-zero correlation would falsify the 'chemical novelty distance' explanation of transfer error. Also compares train GroupKFold RMSE to development RMSE to check whether grouped CV on train is a usable selection proxy. This is diagnostic, unverified reasoning; the analysis is expected to compute, not to improve loss.

findings.interpretation_note: All numbers above are computed from actual train/development rows with the reference HGB hyperparameters; they are diagnostics, not a claim that any representation transfers causally. Learned feature transforms of evaluation inputs were not used here.

steps.hypothesis: Question: for this element-set-disjoint split, where does the HGB reference's 13.38 K development RMSE actually come from? Specifically (a) does the 86-dim stoichiometry vector C carry transferable signal beyond the 81 summary descriptors X (compare identical HGB on X, C, X+C), (b) how much development error is irreducible given only set identity (repeated/contradictory compositions; within-set vs between-set exact residual decomposition), (c) is error concentrated in the high-Tc tail with systematic shrinkage (signed residual by Tc bin; log1p-target control), and (d) does error grow with chemical distance to the nearest training element set (max Jaccard overlap bins, unseen-element rows)? Evidence: the only qualified measurements are median RMSE 36.04, Ridge 18.11 and HGB 13.38 on development; the prior attempt at this diagnostic (idea-048f36) was an operational failure, not a negative result — it aborted in 0.004 CPU s with 'only numpy, sklearn, scipy and math imports supported', so nothing about the error structure has been measured yet. This version uses only numpy/sklearn/math and returns a plain dict. Contrasting outcomes that would change my next move: (1) if HGB on C alone approaches HGB on X, element identity rather than averaged property statistics carries the signal, favoring learned element embeddings / composition kernels; if C alone is far worse and X+C is no better than X, the weighted property statistics are the transferable carrier and adding raw stoichiometry mainly memorizes elements that cannot transfer; (2) if the between-set component dominates total squared error and the oracle set-mean predictor is already near the duplicate noise floor, the leverage is in set-level extrapolation (grouped/robust objectives, chemical-similarity regression), whereas a large within-set component means stoichiometry resolution inside a known set is the weak point; (3) if signed residuals are strongly negative above ~60 K while the log1p control shrinks less at the tail without hurting the bulk, a transformed or two-regime objective is justified; if log1p is uniformly worse, tail shrinkage is information-limited rather than loss-limited; (4) a monotone RMSE increase with decreasing max Jaccard overlap would justify distance-aware weighting/abstention, while flat error across overlap bins would falsify 'chemical distance' as the failure axis. All statements here are unverified expectations; the action only computes numbers, and an analysis is not required to improve loss.

Question: on this element-set-disjoint split, can a representation that goes beyond the 81 fixed summary descriptors X — namely (i) per-element property values recovered by least squares from C and the 'wtd_mean_*' columns of X, used to build fraction-weighted quantiles/range/skew per property, and (ii) explicit composition-shape/doping features (sorted fractions, max/second ratio, Simpson index, dopant counts) — measurably beat the HGB reference's qualified 13.377 K development RMSE, and does blending a C-centric model with X-centric models help? Evidence from the one valid diagnostic (idea-6e4a3e, computed on actual rows): HGB on C alone reached 13.009 K vs 13.377 K on X alone and 13.025 K on X+C, so the fixed summary descriptors are not a sufficient statistic for the stoichiometry vector; the error decomposition shows within-element-set RMSE 10.14-10.22 K dominating between-set 8.13-8.63 K, while the duplicate-composition noise floor is only ~4.3-4.6 K overall (within-duplicate RMSE 7.7-8.3 K), i.e. the largest remaining headroom is within-set, doping-resolved variation that fixed means/entropies of X blur away. The same diagnostic showed a log1p target made things worse (14.52 K, high-Tc signed bias -17.5 K), so the >90 K under-prediction is treated here as ordinary attenuation and is NOT chased with a de-shrinking transform; that is a deliberate counterexample-informed omission. Contrasting outcomes: (1) if the ensemble lands clearly below 13.0 K, non-fixed weighted quantile/shape features carry transferable within-set signal and the next round should ablate which block (property quantiles vs composition-shape) is responsible; (2) if it lands near 13.0 K, the gain is just the already-observed C-vs-X difference plus blending, and richer per-element representations are not the lever; (3) if it is at or above 13.38 K, added features mostly add variance under element-set transfer and the next round should instead attack set-level transfer (e.g. element-similarity kernels or explicit within-set curve models). Unverified expectation, not a measured claim: I expect 12.3-13.0 K. Validity notes: element-set groups for the internal 4-fold CV blend weights are derived from the nonzero pattern of C in train only; the property table, scaler and all models are fit on training rows only, so evaluation features are only transformed by train-fitted maps; predictions are clipped to [0, 1.05*max train Tc] and forced finite. This is an exploratory joint change (new features + ensemble), so it does not by itself attribute credit to individual components.

steps.hypothesis: Question: on this element-set-disjoint split, is the dominant within-element-set error (10.1-10.2 K, per the one valid diagnostic idea-6e4a3e) learnable by an explicit two-stage decomposition — a set-level model predicting the element-set mean Tc from group-centroid features, plus a within-set model predicting deviations from transductively computed group centroids (groups derived from C on the unlabeled evaluation pool, which is allowed and hereby acknowledged) — or is the current single-model route (idea-8300b2, qualified dev RMSE 12.264 K) already capturing everything the decomposition could give? Contrasting outcomes I will treat as decisive: (a) if the two-stage prediction (group model + within model) reaches dev RMSE clearly below the flat HGB on the same feature block computed in the same run, the decomposition is the right structure and the next method round should implement and measure it; (b) if oracle-substitution shows that replacing the predicted group mean by the TRUE dev group mean collapses RMSE toward the ~4.3-4.6 K duplicate noise floor while the fitted group model is the bottleneck, then the headroom is between-set (set-level ranking), not doping resolution, and further doping features are the wrong direction; (c) if replacing the predicted within-deviation by the TRUE deviation barely helps relative to zero deviation, then within-set variation is essentially unpredictable from composition shape at this sample size and the 12.264 K result is near the achievable limit of composition-only transfer; (d) if simply appending group-centered features to the flat model (single-stage transductive centering) matches the two-stage model, the benefit is feature centering rather than target decomposition. Controls in the same run: group-model-only prediction (zero within deviation), agreement between C-derived element-set keys and the supplied groups, dev group-size distribution and pooled within-group label spread, and the split of flat-model error into between-group and within-group parts, so that the oracle numbers are interpreted against actual rows rather than assumed. This analysis is exploratory and its numbers are internal train->development fits, not an officially measured method score.

Question: on this element-set-disjoint split, does explicitly modelling the element-set (group) level separately from within-set doping variation add predictive information beyond a single flat gradient-boosted model, and can an out-of-fold, GROUP-disjoint stacking weight decide that automatically instead of me guessing? Evidence: the only qualified strong method so far (idea-8300b2, dev RMSE 12.264 K, MAE 7.579, group-MAE 6.355) is a flat single-model route; the planned two-stage diagnostic (idea-f56117) never produced data because it was rejected for a disallowed import, so the decomposition claim is currently UNVERIFIED and untested. Rather than spend one of the three remaining rounds on another diagnostic, this method measures the decomposition inside a method run: four candidates (flat HGB on raw Tc; flat HGB on log1p Tc; two-stage = group-centroid model for the set-level mean plus a within-set deviation model on centroid-centred features; ExtraTrees for split-randomisation diversity) are evaluated with GroupKFold over element sets on train only, and combined by non-negative least squares on the out-of-fold predictions. The grouped CV mimics the official transfer protocol, so a candidate that only helps by memorising element sets should receive near-zero weight. Acknowledged transduction: group centroids for the evaluation pool are computed from the unlabeled evaluation features C/X (element-set membership derived from C), which the rules explicitly allow; no evaluation labels, groups, row IDs or formulas are used. Contrasting outcomes declared before execution: (a) if dev RMSE falls clearly below 12.264 K AND the fitted NNLS weight on the two-stage candidate is substantial, the set-level/within-set decomposition carries real transferable structure and round 6 should refine the group-level model; (b) if dev RMSE improves only marginally while the NNLS weight concentrates on the flat raw-target HGB, the gain is ensembling/variance reduction, not decomposition, and the decomposition hypothesis is a negative finding to be reported; (c) if dev RMSE is worse than 12.264 K, the transductive centroids and/or log-target member inject bias under element-set transfer and the flat single-model route should be kept and selected. Because four candidates change jointly, this run cannot attribute each component's contribution by itself; the NNLS weights are diagnostic evidence, not a controlled ablation.

Question: on this element-set-disjoint split, do LEARNED per-element target statistics (composition-weighted aggregates of element-wise log1p(Tc) means/maxima/spreads, computed group-disjoint out-of-fold) carry transferable information beyond the 81 aggregate elemental-property descriptors, or do they merely encode element-set identity and therefore fail exactly on unseen sets? This is the key open question: element SETS are disjoint between train and development, but individual elements overlap heavily, so element-level statistics are the one learned quantity that can legitimately cross the split boundary, while set-level statistics cannot. Evidence: the only qualified strong result is a flat gradient-boosted model on the supplied descriptors (idea-8300b2, dev RMSE 12.264 K, MAE 7.579, group-MAE 6.355); the group/within-set decomposition plus NNLS stacking (idea-b5848e) did NOT reduce RMSE (12.409 K) although it improved group-MAE (6.158), which is consistent with set-level modelling adding little transferable signal. Neither run tested element-level learned encodings, so their value here is UNVERIFIED. Expected contrasting outcomes, predeclared: (1) if element-level encodings are genuinely transferable, the internal GroupKFold ranking will place the X+C+encoding configuration clearly below the X-only configuration and development RMSE should fall below 12.264 K; (2) if the encodings mainly memorise element-set identity, the group-disjoint inner out-of-fold construction will strip their apparent value and the X-only or X+C configuration will win internally, giving development RMSE approximately at or above the flat-model level — a legitimate negative finding that would argue the supplied physical aggregates already saturate element-wise information; (3) an intermediate outcome (encodings win internally but development RMSE does not improve) would indicate that grouped CV on train systematically over-credits element encodings, an important protocol-validity warning for round 7. Novelty indicators (count and mass fraction of evaluation elements rarely or never seen in train) are included so the model can down-weight encodings where transfer is weakest. Configuration choice among four candidates and their pairwise averages is made only from group-disjoint out-of-fold RMSE on train; evaluation features are used solely for learned-transformation-free feature assembly (element encodings are fit on training labels only, then applied to the unlabeled pool), which is acknowledged as an allowed learned transformation with no target lookup.

Question (predeclared): on this element-set-disjoint split, does a heterogeneous ensemble whose blend weights are fitted on GROUP-DISJOINT out-of-fold predictions (i.e. folds split by element set, mimicking the real transfer boundary) reduce development row RMSE below the single flat gradient-boosted descriptor model (idea-8300b2, dev RMSE 12.264 K, MAE 7.579, group-MAE 6.355), and do raw composition fractions / element-presence indicators add transferable signal or merely memorise training element sets? Evidence in context: (a) the best qualified result is a single flat GBM on the 81 descriptors (12.264 K); (b) set-level decomposition with NNLS stacking (idea-b5848e) did NOT improve RMSE (12.409 K) though it improved group-MAE (6.158), suggesting set-level structure adds little transferable RMSE signal while variance-reduction/robustness does help the per-set metric; (c) learned element-level target statistics REGRESSED RMSE (idea-20e93d, 13.441 K), a counterexample showing label-derived element encodings transfer poorly here. Untested and therefore unverified: whether purely feature-side diversity (different target transform, different feature set, different inductive bias: boosted trees vs extremely randomized trees) combined under group-disjoint NNLS weights beats the single GBM. Mechanism claim: RMSE on this split is dominated by a minority of high-Tc cuprate-like rows in unseen element sets; a raw-target model and a log1p-target model make systematically different errors there, so a nonnegative convex-ish blend selected on group-disjoint folds should cut the squared-error tail without the set-identity leakage that hurt idea-20e93d. Expected contrasting outcomes: (1) if feature-side diversity carries transferable information, dev RMSE < 12.26 K with group-MAE not worse than ~6.4; (2) if composition/presence columns mainly encode element-set identity, the blend lands at or slightly above 12.26 K and the outcome replicates the idea-20e93d style failure at a milder magnitude, which would be a further counterexample supporting 'only aggregate elemental-property descriptors transfer'; (3) if the blend improves group-MAE but not RMSE, it reproduces the idea-b5848e pattern and indicates averaging helps small/odd element sets but not the high-Tc tail. Safety: the method is self-contained, uses only numpy/sklearn/scipy, falls back to the best single OOF model if NNLS is degenerate, clips predictions to a finite non-negative range, and is sized (4 folds, 350-iteration HGBs, 200-tree ExtraTrees) to stay well inside the 600 s single-thread deadline. A worse-or-equal result does not overturn the existing best; the automatic lowest-dev-RMSE rule keeps idea-8300b2 if this does not improve.

steps.hypothesis: Question: for predicting Tc on element sets never seen in training, does adding raw stoichiometric identity features (the 86 per-element fractions C) to the 81 summary descriptors X help, or does it mainly let the learner memorize element-set identity that cannot recur across the label-independent element-set hash split, while identity-free chemical-family aggregates (fractions/counts of alkali, alkaline earth, rare earth, 3d/4d/5d transition metals, chalcogen/halogen/pnictogen, group13/14, hydrogen, plus composition entropy, max/second/min fraction, anion ratio) carry the transferable part? Contrasting outcomes that would change my view: (a) if X+C beats X-only under GroupKFold on train element sets and also on development, element identity transfers better than the memorization story predicts; (b) if X+family beats X+C on grouped CV, the transferable signal is coarse chemistry rather than identity, which argues for building later representations from family/periodic aggregates instead of one-hot-like composition columns; (c) if all blocks tie within noise, the 81 descriptors already saturate the information available from formula alone and further gains must come from objective/uncertainty handling, not representation. Also tested in the same run: log1p target training, which should lower MAE on the strongly right-skewed Tc distribution but may raise kelvin RMSE by shrinking high-Tc cuprate predictions; this separates the metric-shaping question from the representation question. Baselines for context are the measured references: median 36.04 K, Ridge 18.11 K, HistGB 13.38 K development RMSE (grouped CV numbers here are train-internal and not directly comparable to those development values). All ablations use the same HistGB hyperparameters and the same 4-fold GroupKFold over train element sets so that only the feature block or target transform varies; the submitted prediction is the combination with lowest out-of-fold RMSE, which is an exploratory joint selection and is reported explicitly in findings.

steps.hypothesis: Question: with the representation held fixed at the parent's best block (81 X descriptors + 86 stoichiometric fractions C + identity-free chemical-family aggregates), is the residual development error on unseen element sets driven by the *learner/loss* rather than by the features? Evidence: idea-ddc787 showed representation changes bought little on top of X+C (family aggregates added only -0.039 K grouped-CV RMSE on top of X+C) and that a log1p target clearly hurt RMSE (+0.716 K), while its prediction distribution (median 24.7 K vs train median 19.8 K, 16.8% below 5 K) suggests a single squared-error HistGB smooths across the strongly bimodal Tc distribution (low-Tc conventional vs high-Tc cuprate/Fe-based regimes). Dev RMSE is currently 13.131 vs the HistGB reference 13.377 (only ~1.8%), well short of the >=5% milestone, so a mechanism-level change is needed. Contrasting outcomes that would change my view: (a) if probability-gated two-regime modelling (HistGB classifier for Tc>=30 K times separate low/high regressors, identical HistGB settings) beats the single HistGB on train GroupKFold and on development, the bottleneck is regime mixing, and later work should refine the gate (threshold, soft mixture, per-regime features); (b) if a mild variance stabilization (sqrt target with second-moment back-correction) beats raw squared error while log1p failed, the failure of log1p was back-transform bias, not target skew per se; (c) if high-variance averaging (ExtraTrees on the same features) matches or beats boosting, extrapolation smoothness across unseen element sets matters more than loss shape; (d) if all variants tie within grouped-CV noise and the NNLS blend gives no gain, the formula-only information is close to saturated for this split and remaining rounds should target uncertainty/abstention or per-element-set structure rather than model class. The per-Tc-bin and per-chemistry-class (cuprate / Fe-based / boride / other-oxide / hydride-like / other) out-of-fold error decomposition reported in findings should tell the project where the kelvin-scale error actually lives and which candidate to refine next. Unverified prior expectation: gating helps most in the 30-100 K band; ExtraTrees helps on sparse chemistries.

steps.hypothesis: Question: on this element-set split, is the residual error dominated by getting the *system level* (element set) wrong rather than the within-system doping trend, and does pooling the unlabeled evaluation rows that share an element set (derived from C, no labels) improve transfer? Evidence from the measured history: the parent idea-af62d4 (dev RMSE 12.495) shows cuprates carry the error mass in train grouped CV (CV RMSE 16.29 K over n=6140 rows, mean y 62.4 K) while 'other' chemistries sit at 3.6 K; row MAE 7.54 exceeds equal-weight group MAE 6.18, i.e. the large, many-row systems (cuprate/Fe-based doping series) are the expensive ones. All prior gains came from learner/loss variation on a flat row-level model (baseline HistGB 13.377 -> 13.131 -> 12.495), and the parent's own note says representation additions on top of X+C bought only -0.039 K in CV; so a flat i.i.d.-row view may be the binding constraint, not the feature list. Mechanism under test: split y into a system-level component (fit HistGB on group-mean features -> group-mean y, weighted by group row count) and a within-system deviation component (fit the identical HistGB on [row-minus-group-mean features, group-mean features] -> y minus group-mean y), then at prediction time reconstruct group means from the unlabeled evaluation features only. Predeclared contrasts, all with representation and learner held fixed: (a) if B_trans beats the matched flat control A_flat in train GroupKFold and on development, error is dominated by system-level placement and averaging sibling rows denoises the chemistry signal, so later rounds should invest in system-level representations/uncertainty; (b) if B_trans ~= C_norow (same fitted models but group means replaced by the row itself, i.e. pooling ablated only), any gain comes from the two-stage target decomposition, not from transduction; (c) if B_trans is worse than A_flat, the group-mean feature vector destroys composition information that the flat model needs (likely visible as a cuprate-class regression), which would be a clean negative result against transductive group pooling and would redirect effort back to per-row loss shaping. Findings also report the between/within variance decomposition of train Tc and train-vs-evaluation group-size distributions, which quantify how much headroom the mechanism can possibly have. Unverified: all internal numbers are train-only grouped CV; only the returned development RMSE is an independent measurement.

findings.design: group key = set of elements with C>0, derived from C on both sides; group model on group-mean features + presence -> group-mean y weighted by row count; deviation model on (row - group mean) + presence -> y - group-mean y; blended with flat HistGB on [X,C]
findings.interpretation: CALCULATED numbers above are train-only out-of-fold; whether the system-level split helps on development is measured separately. If w is near 0 the two-level arm failed and the measurement is effectively the flat learner.
findings.transductive_note: evaluation group means/presence are computed from evaluation features only (no labels, no groups, no ids); train-side CV mimics this by computing held-out group means from held-out features only

steps.hypothesis: Question: on this element-set split, is the residual error dominated by placing the *system* (element set) at the wrong Tc level rather than by the within-system doping trend, and does pooling the unlabeled evaluation rows that share an element set (derived from C only, no labels) improve transfer over a flat row-level model? Evidence: the best measured method (idea-af62d4, dev RMSE 12.495, MAE 7.537, group-MAE 6.176) has row MAE well above equal-weight group MAE, i.e. large many-row doping series (cuprate/Fe-based) carry the error mass, and its own note reported that adding features on top of X+C bought ~0.04 K in grouped CV, suggesting the flat i.i.d.-row view, not the feature list, is the binding constraint. The immediately preceding attempt of exactly this mechanism (idea-6068f5) never produced a measurement: it failed at review/exec with 'only numpy, sklearn, scipy and math imports supported' after 0.004 CPU s, an operational failure, not a negative result about the mechanism. This rerun uses only numpy/sklearn. Mechanism: derive the element-set key from C on both sides; fit (a) a group-level HistGB on group-mean features + presence pattern to group-mean y weighted by group row count, (b) an identical-family HistGB on within-group deviations (row features minus group mean, plus presence) to y minus group-mean y; prediction = group level + deviation. Blend weight w against a flat HistGB on [X,C] is chosen by closed-form least squares on 4-fold GroupKFold out-of-fold predictions clipped at 0, where held-out group means are computed from held-out features only so the CV mimics the transductive evaluation regime. Expected contrasting outcomes: (1) if the system-level hypothesis holds, OOF RMSE of the two-level model beats the flat model and the fitted w lands near 1, with the gain concentrated in cuprate/Fe-based rows that sit in multi-row evaluation groups; (2) if the group-level target is simply harder to predict for unseen element sets, the two-level arm is worse and w collapses toward 0, so blending degenerates to the flat learner and the measured dev RMSE should be near the flat HistGB level, which would be a clean negative for transductive pooling; (3) an intermediate w with per-chemistry gains only in singleton-group rows would indicate the pooling helps mainly through feature smoothing, not through a real system-level effect. Acknowledged: group means and presence patterns of the evaluation pool are learned/derived transformations of evaluation features only, with no target lookup.

findings.design: flat [X|C] rows; base learners = HistGB(raw y), HistGB(log1p y), ExtraTrees; NNLS blend weights fitted on GroupKFold(element-set) OOF; isotonic recalibration of the blend applied only if a nested fold-wise estimate improves train OOF RMSE by >0.02 K
findings.interpretation: CALCULATED values are train-only out-of-fold. If nnls weight on hgb_log is ~0 and isotonic is rejected while top-decile mean_pred is close to mean_y, the tail-shrinkage explanation of the cuprate error mass is not supported and the development measurement should land near the existing flat-model level; the development RMSE reported separately is the only out-of-sample evidence.
findings.transductive_note: no evaluation labels, groups or ids used; evaluation features enter only through the frozen fitted models, no statistics are pooled across evaluation rows

steps.hypothesis: Question: on this element-set split, is the residual error of a flat row-level learner dominated by regression-to-the-mean shrinkage in the high-Tc tail (cuprates), and can a heterogeneous blend (raw-target HistGB + log1p-target HistGB + ExtraTrees) plus an isotonic recalibration of the blend beat the best measured flat method (idea-af62d4, dev RMSE 12.495)? Evidence actually in context: idea-4342ed's train-only OOF decomposition shows error mass concentrated in cuprate rows (OOF RMSE 17.20 at mean y 62.4 K, n=6140) versus 5.70 for 'other' (mean y 6.8 K), while its system-level pooling arm measured WORSE on development (13.398 vs 12.495) even though its own train CV blend looked better (12.94) - so the transductive group-pooling explanation of the gap is contradicted by a real measurement, and a different explanation of the cuprate error mass is needed. Shrinkage is a distinct, testable explanation: squared-loss tree ensembles average toward the conditional mean, and a skewed 0-185 K target makes the top decile systematically under-predicted, which inflates RMSE far more than MAE (consistent with af62d4's row MAE 7.54 against RMSE 12.50). Contrasting outcomes recorded before execution: (a) if shrinkage binds, the nested fold-wise estimate will show isotonic calibration lowering train OOF RMSE, the top-decile mean prediction will sit visibly below the top-decile mean y, the log-target learner will receive nonzero NNLS weight, and development RMSE should drop below 12.495; (b) if instead the flat X+C learner is already near its representational ceiling, NNLS weight will collapse onto hgb_raw, the nested check will reject isotonic (<0.02 K gain), top-decile bias will be small, and development RMSE will land near 12.5 - a counterexample to the shrinkage explanation that would redirect the remaining rounds to representation rather than calibration. Unverified: idea-af62d4's source is not visible here, so this is a new independent flat-model pipeline, not a controlled single-component ablation of it; component attribution inside this run is limited to the in-run OOF comparisons of each base learner, the blend, and the calibrated blend, all computed on train only.

findings.interpretation: CALCULATED numbers above are train-only (out-of-fold over element-set groups) plus descriptive statistics of the prediction vector; they are NOT evaluation-label diagnostics, which this code cannot compute. Decision rule stated before execution: a cuprate-localised drop in oof_rmse_aug supports the missing-carrier-count explanation; |oof_delta| < ~0.1 K in every subset supports the alternative that the symmetric descriptors already carry this information and the cuprate error mass is dominated by scatter from unavailable structure/doping/pressure. Only the separately measured development RMSE is out-of-sample evidence, and a train-OOF gain with no development gain would be a transfer counterexample (as with idea-4342ed).

steps.hypothesis: Question: is the large residual mass measured on high-Tc rows (idea-12a10f train OOF: cuprate RMSE 17.1 at mean y 62.4 K, n=6140; 'other' 5.47 at mean y 6.8 K) caused by the *representation* missing carrier-count/charge-balance information rather than by squared-loss tail shrinkage? Evidence in context: idea-12a10f's decile table shows mean_pred tracking mean_y at every decile (top decile 97.5 vs 99.0) and its NNLS blend with a log1p-target learner plus isotonic recalibration measured 12.634 on development, i.e. WORSE than the best flat method idea-af62d4 (12.495) - so the shrinkage/calibration explanation is contradicted by measurement, and the remaining candidate explanations are (a) missing chemistry-specific information in the 81 symmetric descriptors, or (b) irreducible scatter from unavailable structure/doping/pressure. The 81 X descriptors are means/weighted means/geometric means/entropies/ranges/stds of elemental properties: they are permutation-symmetric statistics and cannot express a nominal charge balance such as the average Cu valence (2+p) in a cuprate or the Fe valence in a pnictide, which is exactly the quantity that orders the doping dome. C gives raw fractions, from which a tree can only reconstruct such a ratio very inefficiently. Test: add ~25 explicitly derived stoichiometry/valence features (net nominal charge, charge per anion, anion/cation ratio, aggregate alkali/alkaline-earth/rare-earth/3d/4d-5d fractions, pnictide and chalcogen fractions, formal Cu valence and hole count p=v_Cu-2, formal Fe valence, O/Cu ratio, element count, max/min fraction, composition entropy, cuprate and Fe-based flags) to the flat [X|C] design and keep the learner, hyperparameters, seeds and CV folds fixed; report train GroupKFold(element-set) OOF RMSE for base vs augmented features overall and split by cuprate / Fe-based / other. Contrasting outcomes recorded before execution: (1) if the augmented design lowers train OOF RMSE mainly inside the cuprate subset AND development RMSE lands below 12.495, explanation (a) is supported and carrier-count information is the missing ingredient; (2) if train OOF is essentially unchanged (|delta| < ~0.1 K) in every chemistry subset, the symmetric descriptors already encode whatever the charge balance adds and the cuprate error mass is better explained by (b) irreducible scatter - a legitimate negative finding that would stop further feature engineering on this axis; (3) if train OOF improves but development RMSE does not beat 12.495, the added features are being exploited in a way that does not transfer to unseen element sets, which is a direct within-run counterexample to the representation hypothesis and mirrors the earlier idea-4342ed case where a better train CV number (12.94) still measured worse on development (13.398). Unverified: I have no prior measurement of these engineered features; nominal oxidation states are a formula-derived proxy, not a physical causal law, and are ambiguous for mixed-valence or pnictide cases.

steps.hypothesis: Question (pre-declared): for transfer to unseen element sets, does the 81-descriptor summary representation X and the raw 86-dim stoichiometry C carry *complementary* predictive information, or is C redundant once X is present? Evidence in context: the measured history shows that every attempt to add hand-built chemistry semantics or target/calibration machinery on top of the flat [X|C] HistGB made development RMSE worse (idea-55db3c 12.796 with +25 charge-balance/valence features vs idea-af62d4 12.495; its own train OOF delta was +0.097 K, i.e. no gain even in-sample; idea-12a10f log1p+isotonic NNLS blend 12.634; idea-4342ed 13.398 was an explicit train-OOF-gain / development-loss counterexample). Those results are consistent with the explanation that the symmetric descriptors already encode the composition chemistry and that residual cuprate error is scatter from unavailable structure/doping/pressure. This proposal tests the remaining untested axis with the learner, folds and seeds held fixed and ONLY the input representation varied, so the contribution of each information source is identified rather than jointly confounded. Contrasting outcomes declared before execution: (a) if hgb_C OOF RMSE is far worse than hgb_X yet NNLS assigns it non-trivial weight and the blend OOF RMSE beats the best single arm by >0.02 K, composition space supplies complementary (non-symmetric) signal and the blend should transfer; (b) if NNLS weight concentrates on hgb_XC and the blend OOF gain is <0.02 K, then X subsumes C and model-diversity averaging is not the missing ingredient — the code then falls back to the single best arm, and a development RMSE at or above 12.495 would be direct evidence that remaining error is representation-independent scatter, not an ensembling deficit. A train-OOF blend gain that does not appear on development would again be a transfer counterexample of the same type as idea-4342ed. Unverified expectation: at most a small gain; the honest outcome may be a negative finding, which is acceptable under the project rules. Automatic round-7 selection still protects the best previously measured method.

steps.hypothesis: Question: does explicit element identity (stoichiometric fractions C, or presence indicators P) carry information beyond the 81 summary descriptors X when the held-out rows are new element SETS? The measured baselines (dev RMSE: median 36.04, Ridge 18.11, HGB 13.38) do not tell us which information the HGB uses or whether identity features help or hurt transfer. Design: the HGB reference configuration (250 iter, lr 0.08, 31 leaves, l2=1) is held fixed and ONLY the feature block varies (X, C, X+C, X+P), evaluated by 5-fold GroupKFold over train element sets (mimics the official partition). The submitted development prediction uses X+C, so the development RMSE versus baseline-2 (13.377) is a single-factor contrast on representation. Predeclared contrasting outcomes: (a) X+C group-CV RMSE lower than X by >0.5 K and development RMSE below 13.38 -> element identity adds transferable information; (b) X+C no better or worse than X -> identity features overfit to training element sets and descriptors already encode what transfers; (c) C alone close to X -> descriptors mostly re-encode identity; (d) C alone far worse than X -> the aggregate property summaries are the transferable representation. Additional calculations in findings (train-only, no evaluation labels): a noise-floor estimate from repeated identical compositions in train with differing Tc (RMSE around per-composition means), out-of-fold error by true-Tc bin (to see whether error is dominated by high-Tc systems), and the list/count of evaluation-pool elements absent from train (derived from inputs.C only). These findings are calculated quantities; their interpretation is unverified until the development score is measured. Expected regression risk: 86 extra sparse columns may reduce HGB generalization to unseen sets; no postprocessing is applied so the contrast stays clean.

steps.hypothesis: Round-1 measured: HGB on X+C reached dev RMSE 13.02 vs 13.38 for X alone (single-factor contrast), with train OOF bias +2.4 K for Tc<10 and -5.0 K for Tc>40 and fold RMSE spread 11.6-14.3. What is NOT known is WHY errors arise for new element sets: are they concentrated on sets with low overlap to train (chemical novelty) or spread across well-covered families (within-system stoichiometry/measurement noise)? And how much of the HGB skill is just identity lookup? This analysis uses actual development rows and the recorded history predictions (baseline-2 HGB-X, idea-b7f89f HGB-XC, and others of matching length) and computes: (1) per dev element set the max Jaccard overlap with any train element set, plus whether a proper subset/superset set exists in train; RMSE stratified by overlap bin; (2) RMSE by chemical family (Cu+O cuprates, Fe pnictide/chalcogenide, Mg-B, other oxides, rest); (3) identity-only controls computed here with no descriptors: Jaccard-kNN over train group-median Tc (k=1,5,20) and composition-space L1 1-NN, and the train-median constant; (4) within-element-set Spearman correlation between prediction and true Tc for sets with >=8 rows (does any model capture doping dependence, or only the level?); (5) dev duplicate-composition noise floor; (6) bias per true-Tc bin on dev. Predeclared contrasting outcomes: (a) RMSE for maxJ<0.5 exceeds RMSE for maxJ>=0.8 by >1.5x -> failure is chemical novelty; next methods should encode element similarity (property-based element embeddings) rather than raw identity; (b) ratios near 1 -> errors dominated by within-family variation; next methods should target stoichiometry-dependent structure and the group-MAE metric. (c) Jaccard-kNN or composition 1-NN within 1 K of HGB-XC 13.02 -> descriptors add little beyond neighbor lookup; (d) they are >3 K worse -> descriptor interpolation is the transferable component. (e) median within-set Spearman <0.3 for all models -> models predict system level, not doping curves; a within-system objective is a candidate. Unverified expectation: cuprates dominate the 40+ K underprediction and identity controls are 2-5 K worse than HGB. This is a diagnostic, not a loss-improving method; its output decides the round-3 method direction.

findings.note: Calculated on actual dev labels. Leaky set-median oracle marks within-set spread only, not an achievable score. Identity controls use no descriptors. Interpretation is separate from these calculations.

steps.hypothesis: Round 2 analysis idea-0dba2f failed operationally (ValueError: only numpy, sklearn, scipy, math imports supported; 0.004 CPU s), so it is not a negative measurement and its question remains open. Measured so far on development: median 36.04, Ridge 18.11, HGB-X 13.38, HGB-X+C 13.02 (single-factor contrast: adding C helps ~0.35 K). Not known: WHY errors arise on new element sets. Question: is dev RMSE of HGB dominated by (a) low-overlap/chemically novel sets, (b) within-set stoichiometry/measurement spread that no set-level predictor can capture, or (c) a few high-Tc cuprate sets with large absolute error? Also: how much of HGB skill is reproduced by identity-only controls with no descriptors (Jaccard-kNN over train set-median Tc, composition L1 kNN)? Contrasting expected outcomes: if per-set MSE correlates negatively with max-Jaccard and RMSE in the <0.34 bin is far above the >=0.8 bin, novelty is the bottleneck and representations that generalize across elements (element-property embeddings, family priors) are the next direction; if within-set RMSE dominates the between/within decomposition and the leaky set-median oracle floor is high (with large duplicate-composition y spread), then remaining error is largely irreducible with these features and the project should target calibrated set-level prediction and robust losses rather than model capacity; if identity controls approach HGB, descriptor skill is mostly lookup; if within-set Spearman between prediction and Tc is near zero, models miss doping dependence and a C-derived stoichiometric representation is warranted. This uses actual dev rows and recorded history predictions of matching length; the set-median oracle is explicitly leaky and reported only as a decomposition. Output: stratified RMSE tables and decompositions to choose the round-4 method direction.

steps.hypothesis: Question: is the remaining development error of HGB-X+C (13.02 K, idea-b7f89f) reducible by a within-set stoichiometry representation, or is it dominated by irreducible within-set label spread? Evidence from idea-b6e07a (calculated on dev labels): within-set RMSE (10.18) exceeds between-set RMSE (8.13); the leaky set-median oracle scores 13.39 K, i.e. worse than HGB, so set-level/identity predictors (Jaccard-kNN 15.6, comp-L1 5nn 14.0) cannot reach the current level and gains must come from modelling stoichiometry inside a set; cuprates (2632 dev rows, RMSE 16.39, ystd 29.3) and six high-overlap cuprate sets (42% of SSE, O-Cu-Y-Ba alone 20% with 720 rows) dominate; high-Tc rows are underpredicted (bias -4.24 for Tc>40). Raw C fractions give trees only axis-aligned splits, whereas cuprate Tc depends on ratios (oxygen per Cu / doping, Ca per Cu ~ CuO2 layer count, alkaline-earth and rare-earth per Cu, Tl/Bi/Hg/Pb block fraction) and Fe-pnictide/MgB2 analogues on Pn/Fe and B/Mg. Method: identical HGB (250 iters, lr 0.08, 31 leaves, l2=1, seed 1729) on X+C plus 33 composition-derived features (element-group fractions, clipped ratios, element count, max fraction, composition entropy, family indicators). Only the feature set changes, so the dev contrast against idea-b7f89f is a single-factor attribution of the representation. Findings report 5-fold GroupKFold-by-element-set CV on train for X+C vs X+C+stoich (overall, cuprate, non-cuprate, high/low-Tc bias) plus an informational sqrt-target variant. Expected contrasting outcomes: (a) dev RMSE drops by >=0.5 K with the largest reduction in cuprate CV error -> ratio representation captures within-set doping/layer structure and the next step is a cuprate-focused representation; (b) no change or worse (<0.2 K either way) while CV also flat -> trees already recover the ratios or within-set spread is measurement noise (dev duplicate-composition y RMS spread 6.72 K), and the next direction should be target/uncertainty handling or bias correction rather than more composition features; (c) CV improves but dev does not -> the ratios overfit train-set idiosyncrasies and do not transfer across element sets. Unverified until measured; no claim of physical causality from formula-derived features.

The seed argument is ignored; HGB uses fixed seed 1729 to match earlier methods. The isotonic map is a learned transformation applied to evaluation-pool predictions; it uses no evaluation labels. Deployed variant is always the isotonic-calibrated one regardless of CV outcome.

steps.hypothesis: Question: the dominant residual mode of the current best methods is systematic underprediction of high-Tc rows (train GroupKFold bias for y>40: -5.10 K for X+C, -4.59 K for X+C+stoich in idea-e70c1e findings; -4.24 K on development per idea-b6e07a), concentrated in cuprates. Two competing explanations: (H1) prediction-space miscalibration: under element-set transfer the tree ensemble shrinks toward the mean so that E[y | pred] > pred for high pred; then a monotone map fitted on train out-of-fold predictions transfers and lowers RMSE. (H2) regression-to-the-mean conditional on y only: E[y | pred] is approximately pred, the y>40 bias exists only when conditioning on the label, and no output mapping can remove it; gains must come from representation (as in e70c1e's stoich features) not from output shaping. Method: identical HGB (250 iters, lr 0.08, 31 leaves, l2=1, seed 1729) on X+C as in idea-b7f89f (13.02 K dev), predictions clipped at 0; 5-fold GroupKFold by element set gives OOF predictions on train; isotonic and linear recalibrators are evaluated with a second-level fold rotation over the OOF predictions (nested, no reuse of the same rows for fitting and scoring); the raw OOF calibration curve (decile mean pred vs mean y, plus 40-60/60-80/80+ bins), cuprate/noncuprate and y- vs pred-conditioned biases are reported as findings. Deployed prediction is always the isotonic-calibrated variant so the development score is a direct contrast to b7f89f with one component changed (clipping at 0 may differ slightly from b7f89f's unseen source). Expected contrasting outcomes: H1 -> top-decile mean y exceeds mean pred by several K, nested isotonic CV RMSE improves by >0.2 K over raw, dev RMSE below 13.02; H2 -> curve near identity, nested calibrated RMSE within +/-0.1 K or worse, dev RMSE ~13.0-13.1 and pred-conditioned bias near zero while y>40 bias persists. Linear vs isotonic separates a global slope/shrinkage from a nonlinear tail effect. Regression risks: isotonic step artifacts and overfitting in sparse high-pred bins, possible increase of cuprate overprediction and of per-element-set MAE; the OOF calibration is fitted under train-internal transfer and may not match train->development transfer. This is unverified until measured; a negative result is informative because it tells the remaining two rounds to spend on representation rather than output correction.

steps.hypothesis: Question: after idea-ef29e2 showed prediction-space recalibration does not help (train GroupKFold RMSE raw 12.95 vs linear 12.96 vs isotonic 13.11; development 13.048 vs 13.025 for the raw X+C model in idea-b7f89f), supporting H2 (E[y|pred] is already ~pred, the y>40 bias of about -5 K is regression-to-the-mean conditional on the label), the remaining route is representation. This tests whether label-derived element-level information transfers across element sets: for each of the 86 elements compute smoothed (m=10) train statistics of Tc among rows containing it (mean Tc, mean log1p Tc, shrunk 75th percentile, log count), aggregated per row as fraction-weighted mean, max, min and unweighted mean over present elements plus two novelty/count features (14 features). Train rows are encoded strictly out-of-fold by element set (GroupKFold 5, nested inside each outer CV fold) so the encoding of a row never sees its own element set, mimicking the evaluation situation; evaluation rows are encoded with full-train statistics (a learned transformation of evaluation features, acknowledged). Controlled contrast: identical HGB (250 iters, lr 0.08, 31 leaves, l2=1, seed 1729, clipped at 0) on X+C versus X+C+elemTE in the same 5 outer folds; findings report paired per-fold RMSE, overall/cuprate/noncuprate/y>40/y<10 subsets and the fraction of evaluation rows containing an element absent from train. Expected contrasting outcomes: (A) elemTE lowers CV RMSE and the y>40 bias by >0.2 K and development loss falls below 13.00 K (current best idea-e70c1e 13.004) -> element-identity-linked Tc statistics carry information the 81 physical descriptor summaries and raw fractions do not expose to the trees under transfer; (B) no change -> X/C already encode this and the tree recovers element identity from C; (C) CV improves but development does not, or CV worsens -> OOF-encoding noise or train(OOF, 4/5 data)/eval(full-train) encoding mismatch dominates. Deployed variant is pre-declared as X+C+elemTE regardless of CV outcome. Exploratory; no guarantee of improvement.

steps.hypothesis: Question: is the residual development error of the plain X+C HGB (idea-b7f89f 13.025; idea-798374 base arm train GroupKFold 12.95, per-fold RMSE spread 11.6-14.3) partly model variance that transfers to new element sets, or is it dominated by bias/irreducible heterogeneity (cuprate CV RMSE 17.2 vs noncuprate 6.8, y>40 bias +5 K that idea-ef29e2 showed recalibration cannot remove, element target encoding in idea-798374 not helping: dev 13.25 vs 13.02)? Test: hold the model, features (X+C), hyperparameters and clipping identical to the idea-798374 base arm, and change only the fitting procedure to an average of HGBs fit on element-set (group) bootstrap resamples, so each member omits ~37% of train systems, mimicking the unseen-element-set situation. Controlled contrast inside the run: single HGB vs 6-member group-bag on the same GroupKFold(5) folds (all/cuprate/noncuprate/y>40/y<10), plus per-fold deltas and OOF prediction agreement. Deployed (pre-declared regardless of CV): 10-member group-bag on full train. Expected contrasting outcomes: (A) variance matters -> development RMSE below ~12.9 with per-fold deltas consistently negative and lower cuprate RMSE; (B) bias dominates -> development RMSE within about +/-0.05 of 13.02, deltas mixed like the TE arm, high OOF agreement (corr>0.99), meaning further gains need different information (structure/pressure are unavailable) rather than variance reduction. If B, the plateau across idea-b7f89f/e70c1e/ef29e2/798374 is a substantive negative finding for this split, and automatic selection of the lowest valid development RMSE (currently idea-e70c1e 13.004) remains appropriate. Unverified until measured; no pretense this exceeds the 5% confirmation milestone.

steps.hypothesis: Question: before proposing a new representation, what limits the HGB(X) reference (dev RMSE 13.38, MAE 8.46, group-MAE 7.57 vs Ridge 18.11 and median 36.04) under the element-set-disjoint split, and which information (81 elemental-property summaries X vs 86 stoichiometric fractions C vs both, raw vs log1p target) transfers? Calculations: (1) noise floor from repeated identical compositions in train (leave-one-out same-composition RMSE), which bounds achievable row RMSE independent of model; (2) heuristic C-derived families (Cu&O, Fe, other) train/dev shift; (3) element coverage: dev rows containing elements absent/rare in train; (4) kNN-by-cosine-on-C control and HGB(X) dev error stratified by max cosine similarity to train, true-Tc bin, family, element coverage and top-5% error concentration, using the official idea-baseline-2 dev prediction from history if present (else a labelled refit); (5) GroupKFold-5 on train plus dev fit for HGB on X, C, X+C, X+C-log1p with identical HGB settings, so representation is the only varied component. Contrasting expected outcomes: (a) if C-only or X+C clearly beats X on both group-CV and dev, the descriptor summaries discard transferable stoichiometric information and the next method should learn element-wise/compositional representations; if C-only is much worse, element identity does not transfer to new element sets and X-style property aggregates are the right basis; (b) if error is concentrated in low-similarity or unseen-element rows and in high-Tc bins, failure is extrapolation and calls for similarity-aware shrinkage or family-conditional models; if error is spread evenly and the repeated-composition noise floor is large (several K), remaining gains are bounded by label noise and a >=5% RMSE improvement claim needs caution; (c) log1p target trading lower MAE for higher RMSE would argue against it for the official loss. Findings are calculated on actual rows; family labels are heuristic, not chemical ground truth. This analysis does not change loss; it decides the direction of round-2 methods. Unverified until executed.

steps.hypothesis: Round-1 analysis idea-088ed6 failed operationally (ValueError: only numpy, sklearn, scipy and math imports supported) before any computation; that is not a negative measurement, so the questions remain open. Question: what limits the HGB(X) reference (dev RMSE 13.38 / MAE 8.46 / group-MAE 7.57 vs Ridge 18.11, median 36.04) under the element-set-disjoint split, and which information transfers? Calculations on actual rows: (1) leave-one-out RMSE among identical train compositions (label noise floor independent of model); (2) C-derived heuristic families (Cu&O, Fe, other) train/dev proportions and Tc levels; (3) dev rows containing elements absent or rare (<5 systems) in train; (4) HGB(X) refit with the reference settings (seed 1729) on train, dev error stratified by true-Tc bin, family, max cosine similarity of C to train, element coverage, signed bias per bin, top-5% SSE share and worst dev systems, plus kNN-cosine-on-C controls and a check against the stored idea-baseline-2 prediction if present in history; (5) GroupKFold(3) on train and train->dev fits for HGB on X, C, X+C, X+C with log1p target, identical HGB settings so representation is the only varied component. Contrasting expected outcomes: (a) C-only or X+C beats X on both group-CV and dev -> the 81 summaries discard transferable stoichiometric information and a composition-aware representation is the next method; (b) X beats C and X+C does not help -> element-identity features overfit train systems and the next method should target where X fails (e.g. high-Tc bins, cuprates, low-similarity rows); (c) the within-repeat LOO RMSE is a large fraction of 13.38 -> the remaining headroom is small and group-MAE or robustness, not row RMSE, is the realistic target; (d) log1p lowers MAE but raises RMSE -> target transform trades the high-Tc tail against the bulk. Unverified until executed; findings are calculations, interpretations will be labelled.

Question: does adding explicit, composition-derived chemical-family aggregate features to X+C improve transfer to unseen element sets beyond what the tree model already extracts from raw C/X? Evidence from idea-cdf6fc (calculated on actual rows, HGB settings identical to idea-baseline-2): dev RMSE C=13.009, XC=13.025, X=13.377 (train GroupKFold3 OOF: XC 13.27 < C 13.52 < X 13.83), so composition identity transfers at least as well as the 81 property summaries; dev error is dominated by the C-derived CuO family (RMSE 16.79 vs 6.31 for 'other'), the top 5% of rows carry 54.5% of SSE, and predictions are biased low by 11.1 K for true Tc>=90 K. kNN on cosine(C) is much worse (15.1-17.5), so plain composition-similarity memorization does not transfer, but tree partitions of C do. Interpretation (unverified): trees approximate sums/ratios of many sparse C columns poorly, so family-level quantities (alkaline-earth/rare-earth/chalcogen/pnictogen sums, O/Cu ratio, Cu vs cation-site ratio, cuprate and Fe-pnictide/chalcogenide indicators, element count, max fraction, composition entropy) may let the model share statistics across element sets that differ only by substitution within a family, which is exactly how dev systems relate to train systems (all dev elements present in train). Held fixed: HGB hyperparameters (250 it, lr 0.08, 31 leaves, l2 1, seed 1729), training pool, no target transform; the only varied component is the appended feature block F, so the contrast is against XC=13.025 and C=13.009. Expected contrasting outcomes: dev RMSE clearly below ~12.7 with group-MAE not worse than 7.04 supports that family-level aggregates carry transferable information the raw representation does not expose; RMSE ~13.0 (within the C/XC spread) means the tree already recovers this information and the representation direction is exhausted at this model capacity; RMSE worse than 13.4 would indicate the aggregates encourage overfitting to train-family levels under the observed family shift (CuO 48.6% train vs 56.3% dev rows, dev CuO Tc mean 55.7 vs train 62.4). Official scoring also reports the per-Tc-bin behaviour only indirectly; a later analyze action can compare this method's stored dev predictions with the HGB(X) bias by Tc bin. This is a single method measurement, not a discovery claim; the label-noise floor among repeated train compositions (LOO RMSE 9.7) bounds what any method can achieve.

Question: which learned representation of composition transfers to unseen element sets? idea-cdf6fc (analysis, computed on actual dev rows, not a qualified method score) found HGB on C alone (13.01) transfers at least as well as X (13.38) or X+C (13.03), while kNN on cosine(C) fails (15.1-17.5); the best measured method so far is idea-5bdb4a at 13.30 (family features), so explicit hand-built family aggregates did not clearly beat raw C. Competing explanations: (H1) trees succeed because axis-aligned thresholds on dominant fractions (Cu, O, Ba, Fe...) capture doping-like regimes, and any element-identity model without partition structure will overfit element sets like kNN did; (H2) a smooth distributed representation (first layer = learned element embedding, weighted by fraction) can share statistics across substitutions within families and transfer at least as well as trees. Test: 4-seed-averaged MLPRegressor (256,128 relu, adam) on [C, sqrt(C)] with y standardized, early stopping on a 10% element-set holdout derived from train C (not a random row split, to avoid within-set leakage), predictions clipped at 0. Predeclared contrasting outcomes: dev RMSE <= ~13.0 supports H2 (distributed composition representation is a viable transfer basis, candidate for later selection/ensembling); RMSE >= 14 supports H1 (partition structure, not just C information, drives transfer); ~13-14 suggests representation form matters less than information content. Caveats: seed averaging, sqrt(C) augmentation and group-holdout early stopping are all part of this method, so a win is not attributable to the MLP alone; a fair follow-up would seed-average HGB on C. Reference figures from idea-cdf6fc are analysis computations; this proposal's own hypothesis is unverified until measured.

Question: after idea-ed09ee (measured 15.42) refuted the distributed-embedding MLP alternative (H2) and confirmed that axis-aligned tree models on composition transfer best (H1), what limits tree transfer to unseen element sets: variance from fitting element-set-specific structure, or bias from Tc regimes absent in train? Evidence: idea-cdf6fc (analysis on actual dev rows, not a qualified method score) reported single HGB on C = 13.01 and on X+C = 13.03, versus the measured baseline-2 HGB on X = 13.38 and idea-5bdb4a family features = 13.30 (measured). Single HGB fits are trained on rows, but the evaluation unit is a new element set; if a large share of dev error comes from trees latching onto set-idiosyncratic splits, then averaging K=8 HGB models each fit on a bootstrap over element sets (sets derived label-independently from the support pattern of C in train, resampled with replacement and applied as sample weights; fixed 300 iterations, early stopping disabled because set-bootstrap weights would corrupt HGB's internal random validation split) should reduce dev RMSE. Predeclared contrasting outcomes: (a) dev RMSE clearly below ~12.8 (below both the 13.01 analysis figure and 13.30 measured best) supports variance-limited transfer and makes set-level bagging a candidate for selection; (b) RMSE within ~13.0-13.4 means bagging adds nothing over a single tree ensemble and the residual is dominated by bias (compositions whose Tc regime is not represented in train), redirecting the last rounds toward per-set residual diagnostics rather than ensembling; (c) RMSE worse than 13.4 would indicate the set-bootstrap discards too much training coverage (each replica sees ~63% of sets), a negative result about data scarcity per set. Caveat: this is an exploratory joint change relative to the measured baseline-2 (features X -> C+X plus bagging); the bagging effect is isolated only relative to the unqualified 13.03 analysis figure for X+C. Predictions clipped at 0 and any non-finite value replaced by the training median. No learned transformation of evaluation features beyond model prediction; C+X are used as given.

Question: idea-a1d17c (measured dev RMSE 12.97, K=8 set-bootstrap HGB, 300 iterations, early stopping off, composition C as features per its stated design) fell short of its own predeclared 'clearly below ~12.8' variance-explanation threshold, so residual error on unseen element sets is at least partly not bootstrap-reducible variance. Candidate cause: trees on raw C must re-learn each element's marginal association with Tc from splits on that element's fraction, which is fragile when the element appears in new combinations. This method holds the a1d17c training recipe fixed (same K=8 set-bootstrap sample weights derived label-independently from the support pattern of C, 300 iterations, lr 0.08, 31 leaves, l2 1.0, early stopping disabled, C retained as raw features) and changes exactly one component: 14 appended element-level target-statistic features (composition-weighted mean, max and min over present elements of each element's smoothed mean Tc, mean log1p Tc, 90th-percentile Tc and Tc std, plus weighted-mean and min log training count of present elements). Leakage control: training-row encodings are computed out-of-fold with 5 folds over element SETS (a set never contributes to its own encoding), evaluation encodings use all training rows; this train/eval mismatch is an acknowledged learned transformation of evaluation features and a possible regression source. Predeclared contrasting outcomes: (a) dev RMSE <= ~12.7 supports that additive element-marginal information transfers to new element sets beyond what trees extract from C; (b) ~12.85-13.05 means the trees already capture element marginals and the bias lies elsewhere (e.g., Tc regimes absent in train); (c) > 13.1 is a negative result indicating the OOF-encoding noise or the elemental-marginal prior hurts transfer. Dev RMSE is not the confirmation metric; the 5% milestone (~12.71 relative to baseline-2's 13.38) is only a rough dev-side target. Unverified until measured.

Question: measured history shows K=8 set-bootstrap HGB on X+C (idea-a1d17c, dev RMSE 12.97) improved over single HGB (baseline-2, 13.38) by ~0.4 K, but adding element-level target statistics (idea-6b5681, 13.37) made it worse, and it missed its own ~12.8 variance-explanation threshold. Remaining error on unseen element sets may be (a) shared bias that any tree learner on these descriptors reproduces, or (b) learner-specific variance that heterogeneous averaging can cancel where homogeneous bootstrap cannot. This method keeps the a1d17c training recipe as described in its hypothesis (K=8 label-independent set-bootstrap weights from the support pattern of C, 300 iterations, lr 0.08, 31 leaves, l2 1.0, early stopping off, X+C as features; note this is my reimplementation from the described recipe, not the identical source) and appends one different learner family, an ExtraTreesRegressor (200 trees, max_features 0.5, min_samples_leaf 2) on the same X+C, blended with predeclared fixed weights 0.6 HGB / 0.4 ET, predictions clipped at 0 K. Weights and clip are predeclared, not tuned on development. Expected contrasting outcomes: dev RMSE clearly below ~12.7 supports (b), heterogeneous diversity reducing transfer error beyond bootstrap; RMSE near 12.97 or above supports (a), remaining error is shared descriptor-limited bias, and the automatic selection should keep a1d17c. Caveats: only the blend is measured, not ET alone, so the ET-alone contribution is not identified; group MAE will be compared to a1d17c's 6.91 to check the blend does not trade row RMSE for worse per-set error. This is the last research round; if the blend is not better on development, official selection falls back to a1d17c by lowest valid dev RMSE, so this test is selection-safe apart from the usual risk that a small dev gain does not persist on confirmation.

scope: One pair per model on one public materials dataset with element-set-disjoint split. Exploration and model selection are not proof of physical mechanism, literature novelty, or stable general research capability. Findings require separate semantic review.
